title: Postural (Orthostatic) Hypotension
subject: Medicine
summary: A fall in blood pressure on standing caused by inadequate autonomic or volume compensation. Recognise the bedside test, common tropical causes, and manage with fluids, compression and careful drug choice.

sections.p: A sustained drop in systolic ≥20 mmHg or diastolic ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing (or head‑up tilt) with associated symptoms.
b: Measure BP supine after 5 min rest, then at 1 and 3 min after standing.
Ask about dizziness, light‑headedness, visual blur, syncope.

sections.p: Stage I: systolic drop 20‑29 mmHg or diastolic 10‑19 mmHg; Stage II: systolic ≥30 mmHg or diastolic ≥20 mmHg; Stage III: symptomatic collapse or need for emergency care.
b: Stage guides urgency of fluid resuscitation and monitoring.

sections.p: Classify by volume depletion, autonomic failure, medication, and secondary disease.
b: Volume depletion – diarrhoea, malaria, severe anaemia, vomiting, poor oral rehydration.
Autonomic neuropathy – diabetes, HIV, chronic alcohol, peripheral neuropathy from antiretrovirals.
Medications – low‑potency antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, quetiapine), antihypertensives, diuretics.
Cardiac – severe aortic stenosis, heart failure with low output.
Infections – TB meningitis, chronic hepatitis B with cirrhosis, schistosomiasis‑related portal hypertension.

sections.p: Patients report dizziness on standing, blurred vision, fatigue, or syncope. Physical exam shows tachycardia, cold clammy skin if hypovolaemic, and a delayed rise in BP.
b: Orthostatic test positive when symptoms accompany the BP fall.
Look for signs of dehydration: dry mucosa, reduced skin turgor, sunken eyes.

t.b: Confirms orthostatic fall; if unavailable, use manual cuff with timed readings.
Detects anaemia, infection, or eosinophilia from parasitic disease.
Assesses volume status and renal contribution.
Excludes hypoglycaemia as a cause of dizziness.
Looks for bradyarrhythmia or conduction block that can mimic orthostatic drop.

sections.p: Severe falls can cause head injury; prolonged hypoperfusion may precipitate myocardial ischaemia or stroke in high‑risk patients.
b: Syncope with chest pain or palpitations → urgent cardiac review.
Persistent tachycardia >120 bpm with hypotension → consider sepsis or adrenal crisis.

sections.p: Treat underlying cause, restore intravascular volume, and use non‑pharmacologic measures before drugs.
b: Oral rehydration solution (ORS) for mild‑moderate dehydration; IV crystalloids (normal saline) if vomiting or severe volume loss.
Compression stockings (30‑40 mmHg) to reduce venous pooling.
Educate slow positional changes; raise head of bed 10‑20°.
Review medications – stop or replace chlorpromazine, quetiapine, diuretics if possible.
Midodrine (α‑agonist) only if non‑pharmacologic measures fail and no severe cardiac disease.
Fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid) for neurogenic cases with low aldosterone, avoiding in heart failure.

sections.p: Re‑measure orthostatic vitals after each intervention; aim for no symptomatic drop. Counsel on adequate fluid intake, salt supplementation where safe, and avoidance of precipitating drugs.
b: Schedule review within 1 week for acute cases, then monthly until stable.
In chronic autonomic failure, involve physiotherapy for tilt‑training.

sections.p: Conditions that cause dizziness but have different mechanisms.
b: Cardiac syncope – arrhythmia or outflow obstruction; pulse often irregular or absent.
Vasovagal faint – prodrome of nausea, warm skin, bradycardia; BP fall is abrupt after trigger.
Cerebral hypoperfusion from anemia – no orthostatic change, improves with transfusion.

sections.p: Certain tests may appear normal despite significant orthostatic fall.
b: Normal resting BP does not exclude orthostatic hypotension; always perform standing measurements.
Serum sodium may be normal in early dehydration; rely on clinical signs.

whenToSeekHelp: Syncope with chest pain, palpitations or dyspnoea
Persistent systolic BP <90 mmHg while standing
New neurological deficits after a fall

faq.q: Why does standing cause a blood pressure drop?
faq.a: Gravity pools blood in the legs, reducing venous return; if the autonomic system or volume cannot compensate, BP falls.

faq.q: Can antipsychotics really cause orthostatic hypotension?
faq.a: Yes; low‑potency agents like chlorpromazine block α‑adrenergic receptors, blunting vasoconstriction on standing.

faq.q: Is it safe to give fluids to a patient with heart failure who has orthostatic hypotension?
faq.a: Give cautious, low‑volume boluses and monitor for pulmonary oedema; consider compression stockings and medication adjustment first.

exam: What bedside test confirms orthostatic hypotension and how is it performed? — Measure supine BP after 5 min rest, then standing BP at 1 and 3 min; look for ≥20 mmHg systolic or ≥10 mmHg diastolic drop with symptoms.

A patient on chlorpromazine presents with dizziness on standing. How do you manage the drug issue? — Review necessity, taper or switch to a drug with less α‑blockade; if essential, add compression stockings and monitor BP.

How would you differentiate neurogenic orthostatic hypotension from hypovolaemia in a malaria‑endemic area? — Neurogenic shows minimal heart‑rate increase (<15 bpm) on standing; hypovolaemia shows tachycardia >20 bpm and improves with fluids.

What are the first‑line non‑pharmacologic measures for an acute orthostatic episode in a rural clinic? — Slow position changes, oral rehydration with salt, compression stockings, and review of offending meds.

When is midodrine indicated and what are its contraindications? — Use after failure of fluids and compression in persistent symptomatic orthostatic hypotension; avoid in severe cardiac disease, supine hypertension, or pheochromocytoma.

A patient collapses after standing, BP 85/50, pulse 130, and has a fever. What urgent steps do you take? — Treat as possible sepsis: give IV crystalloids, obtain cultures, start broad‑spectrum antibiotics, and monitor cardiac status.
Why might a normal resting ECG not rule out orthostatic hypotension? — ECG assesses rhythm, not autonomic vascular response; orthostatic drop can occur with a normal sinus rhythm.

Explain why compression stockings are preferred over leg elevation in low‑resource settings. — Stockings are cheap, easy to apply, maintain venous return continuously, and do not require a bed‑side assistant.
